opening.headline: We examine why the model loses track of what is happening and costs rise as the conversation becomes longer, from the perspective of a finite resource called context.
body: After dozens of conversations with an agent, you'll end up breaking the rules you set out in the first place, being noticeably slower to respond, or driving up your bill. It's not that the model has suddenly gone bad, it's often the result of a lack of control over what we show the model.

In this class, you will learn what context engineering is, why the context window is a finite resource, and how to decide what to put in and what to leave out. At the end, we will solve how we can redesign an agent that contains 50 search results.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the purpose and principles of context engineering
You can distinguish between what to put in the context and what to leave out.

screens.title: What happens the longer the conversation goes on
screens.lead: This is a common situation when working with an agent for a long time. Read the scene below and think about what the problem is. The contents corresponding to the ‘see cause’ in the picture are explained in the paragraph below.

visual.alt: A scene with a long conversation thread on the left and two speech bubbles on the right.
labels: Increased cost: complete re-entry for each request

paragraphs: A team has been working with a coding agent for dozens of turns. At first, we set a rule of “write tests first”, but at some point the agent starts not following this rule. Responses become increasingly slower, and the token cost charged for each request rises.

Each time the agent calls the tool, it receives results, and the results are added to the conversation. And every time you send the next request, the entire stack goes back into the model. System instructions, tool definitions, tool results, and message records are all delivered to the model as one piece.

So has the model become dumb, or has it mismanaged the context? This lesson focuses on the second possibility. Even if the model is the same, the results vary greatly depending on how the content shown to the model is structured.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Will this problem go away if I switch to a model with larger windows? You will be able to answer this question again at the end of class.

screens.outro: First, let me think about whether I have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think about it: Have you ever seen a situation like this?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced a model forgetting instructions given earlier during a long conversation?
items.answer: This is common. Rather than saying that the model forgets the instructions, it often happens that the information ahead becomes relatively blurred as the input becomes longer. In this lesson, the reason is explained through the concept of attention.

items.prompt: Have you ever encountered a situation where an agent is loading entire file contents or search results, resulting in slow response?
items.answer: The results the tool retrieves are stacked in the context and re-entered on each subsequent request. One big result affects the cost and delay of all subsequent turns.

items.prompt: Was there a moment when you thought, ‘If the window gets bigger, this will solve the problem’?
items.answer: As the window gets bigger, you can put in more, but the more you put in, the more the precision gradually decreases. So what to put in becomes a more important question than how much you can put in.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's start by defining what context engineering is.

screens.title: What is Context Engineering?
screens.lead: Compare the scope differences between prompt engineering and context engineering by switching between the two states.

visual.alt: A schematic showing all components, with the prompt in a small circle and the context in a large circle surrounding it.

states.label: Show only prompts
states.body: Prompt engineering is all about using the instructions given to the model, especially system prompts. The focus is on refining which representations lead the model's behavior in the desired direction. The scope is close to a single text handed to the model. For one-off questions, this perspective is often sufficient.

states.label: See full context
states.body: Context refers to all of the tokens that the model samples when creating a response. Context engineering is about shaping this entire set of tokens, including system instructions, tools, MCP (standard conventions for connecting external tools and data to agents), external data, and even message records. As the agent loops, the information available for the next turn continues to increase, so it has to repeatedly filter out what to put into the window. The key question is which context configuration best elicits the desired behavior.

screens.outro: Now that we've defined the scope, let's look at why we need to do this through the model's attention limits.

screens.title: Context Window Limits: Your Attention is Your Budget
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the context length. The explanation changes as to how the precision and attention of the model varies depending on its length.

visual.alt: A gently curved graph in which accuracy gradually decreases as the number of tokens increases.
labels: Not a cliff but a gentle slope

stops.body: When there are few tokens, the model can attend to all information relatively evenly. The ability to accurately recall information ahead remains high. However, even at this point, unnecessary content obscures the signal, so screening is necessary.

As the number of tokens increases, the ability to accurately recall the preceding information gradually decreases. This phenomenon is called context rot. In Transformer, every token looks at every other token, so if there are n tokens, there will be n² relationships. As relationships increase, attention becomes thinly spread.

Even in long contexts, the model may be competent, but with lower precision. The drop appears as a gentle slope rather than a cliff. Explain that although the degree of slope varies from model to model, this property is present in all models.

Let’s look at the structure a little more to see why this happens. Transformer's attention is a method of weighting how much each token references other tokens. As the number of tokens increases, the attention that one token can share becomes thinner. In experimental studies, it has been observed that accuracy drops noticeably when the information needed for a question is in the middle of the input rather than at the beginning or end, a phenomenon called lost in the middle. However, the degree of this location bias varies depending on the model and task, so specific numbers should not be generalized. Use it as a placement check to ensure important instructions and evidence are not buried in the middle of lengthy context.

Context is a finite resource of diminishing marginal utility. Just as humans have limits to working memory, models have attentional budgets. The goal is not to put in a lot, but to create the smallest set of high-signal tokens that will produce the desired result.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the limitations, let's take a component-by-component look at what a good context looks like.

ext.title: Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017)
Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (2023)

screens.title: What to put in and what to take out
screens.lead: Select each tab to check the criteria for what to include and what to exclude for each component.

tabs.label: system prompt
tabs.body: You need to find the right balance between a long list of overly tangled if-else rules and giving only vague, high-level guidance. Be too specific and it's brittle, and be too vague and the model won't get the signal it needs. The goal is to sufficiently describe expected behavior with minimal information. Minimum does not mean short.

tabs.label: tools
tabs.body: You should avoid bloated tool sets that have overlapping functions or that make it difficult for people to know for sure which tool to use in which situation. Tools must have a clear purpose without overlapping with each other, and the results they return must also be in a form that saves tokens. This is because both tool definitions and results take context.

tabs.label: example
tabs.body: Avoid listing every exception as an example. Instead, pick a few diverse, standard examples that represent the expected behavior. For the model, examples are a means of conveying the behavior you want to show like a picture, so it is important to choose them well rather than adding too many.

tabs.label: principles
tabs.body: Keep the context both rich and tight. It must contain the information necessary for the decision at this stage, and must not contain information that is not necessary. There is only one criterion for judgment. The question is whether this token is really needed for the next decision.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at static configuration, let's move on to how information is retrieved during execution.

screens.title: JIT context: carrying only identifiers
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the method of loading everything in advance and loading it when needed.

visual.alt: A two-line diagram comparing the contents of a window in prepackaged and JIT methods.

states.label: Put everything in advance
states.body: This method processes all data in advance and puts it into context. It has the advantage of being fast, like a pre-computed search. But the window is filled with more content than necessary, re-entered every turn, increasing costs and delays, and burying important signals.

states.label: JIT (fetch when needed)
states.body: It only retains lightweight identifiers such as file paths, saved queries, and web links, and allows tools to load the data into context at runtime when needed. When Claude Code analyzes large amounts of data, it uses target queries and does not load the entire data using commands such as head and tail. Metadata such as file names, folder structures, and times are used as clues to navigate incrementally. There is also a price. Runtime searches are slower than precomputed searches, and require well-designed tools and instructions. A realistic solution is a hybrid. Put CLAUDE.md in advance and find the rest with glob and grep.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the single-call design, let's look at an example of how to flip windows in a very long operation.

screens.title: Commentary: Separate subagents to hold up long tasks
screens.lead: Your instructor will walk you through the sequence in which subagent separation works. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: A schematic where the main agent delegates work to two sub-agents and only receives a summary in return.
labels: Explore tens of thousands of tokens

steps.title: Primary agents divide the work
steps.body: If you complete a long task in one context, the window will quickly fill up. So the main agent leaves narrow, well-defined tasks to specialized sub-agents. Subagents start with a clean context.

steps.title: Subagent explores deeply
steps.body: Subagents spend tens of thousands of tokens and can read files, search, and call tools. This detailed navigation context is isolated within a subagent and does not occupy the main agent's window.

steps.title: Only the summary comes back
steps.body: When the sub-agent is finished, it returns a summary of usually 1,000 to 2,000 tokens back to the main agent. The primary agent can focus on synthesizing and analyzing these results.

steps.title: Other means are also used
steps.body: There are other means of crossing the same limits. There is compression, which summarizes conversations as the window fills and continues in a new window, and clearing out old tool results is the lightest compression. Alternatively, agents can write down progress in an external notebook, such as NOTES.md, and read it again when necessary.

screens.outro: Now that we've covered all the concepts, let's work through a concrete example step by step.

screens.title: Explanatory example: When 50 search results are entered as is
screens.lead: The instructor explains a case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: A bar comparing the context window usage when 50 search results were entered and after improvements.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The research agent invoked the search tool and received 50 results, putting the entire text of each result into context. Subsequent answers are built on this context.

steps.title: Stage 1: Important signals are buried
steps.body: Most of the window is filled with irrelevant text. The goals and instructions initially given become relatively buried, and it becomes difficult for the model to determine what is important.

steps.title: Stage 2: Costs and delays pile up
steps.body: Starting from the next turn, these 50 items will be re-entered for each request. Costs and delays increase, and precision decreases due to context rot. This is why it does not work even if the window is large.

steps.title: Step 3: Improvement direction
steps.body: Open only what you need, leaving only identifiers such as titles and links. This is the JIT context. Detailed navigation is left to sub-agents and only a summary is received.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment criteria
steps.body: Every decision boils down to one question: Is this token really needed for the next decision? If necessary, add it; if not, replace it with an identifier or remove it.

screens.outro: Now that we've analyzed the cause of the bad configuration, we'll outline an improvement design in the next screen.

data.notes: All improvements in the table do not change the model, only the context configuration. Even after improvement, necessary information must be included, so the goal is not to reduce it unconditionally. Compression can also cause information to be lost in the summarization process, so it is important to leave decisions and unresolved issues in the summary. When making design changes, it is safer to check one by one to see which changes affected response quality and token usage, rather than changing everything at once. The number of rationale items in the After Improvement column is not a set value, but depends on the stage of work.

screens.outro: I will gather the analysis and summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Select sentences and match them with terms
screens.lead: When you select each summary sentence, an explanation of the associated term will appear. There is nothing to enter or submit.

items.prompt: Context is a finite resource, and as tokens increase, marginal utility decreases.
items.answer: Related terms are context window and context rot. The context window is the range of tokens that the model processes at once, and context rot is a phenomenon in which the ability to accurately recall preceding information decreases as the number of tokens increases. Even if the window doesn't fill up, the longer it is, the more distracting it becomes.

items.prompt: The goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens that will produce the desired result.
items.answer: A related term is context engineering. It involves curating and maintaining a set of tokens at the point of inference, including all system instructions, tools, external data, and message records. The criterion is whether this token is needed for the next decision.

items.prompt: The JIT context makes the window lighter by leaving only the identifier and loading it when needed.
items.answer: Carry around file paths, saved queries, and links and import them into the tool. Navigation is slower, so a hybrid like CLAUDE.md, where you pre-fill the necessary information and then search for the rest, is realistic.

items.prompt: Subagent separation isolates detailed navigation and returns only the summary
items.answer: A clean context subagent will spend tens of thousands of tokens to explore, and only return a summary of 1,000 to 2,000 tokens to the main agent. The primary agent focuses on synthesis and analysis. Tokens written by subagents do not accumulate in the main agent's window, so the main agent's judgment is not impaired even during long tasks.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's think about it in relation to our own work.

screens.title: Connect to my work
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read the questions and think for yourself. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Key terms covered in this lesson are context window, context engineering, context rot, JIT context, and subagent separation. Think about where each one touches on the agent you are using.

For example, you can check whether the agent you are using is accumulating tool results as is, whether the rules you initially set are not blurred in a longer conversation, or whether you are neglecting selection because the window has become larger.
Good context design is not a one-time thing. As the agent loops and continuously changes context, it must repeatedly decide what information to keep and what to discard.

The final criterion to remember is simple. Every token you put into context should contribute to the next decision, as much as it costs money and attention. Options learned in this class include converting tokens that do not contribute to identifiers, leaving them to sub-agents, reducing them through compression, or removing them altogether. The four are not mutually exclusive, so they are often used together within one agent. Which option is right for you will depend on how often and how accurately you need the information.

callout.label: Questions to Think About
callout.text: Where does my work get stuck with context window limitations? If you have a scene that comes to mind, think about which method would be most appropriate.

checks.q: What is the most appropriate reason why the ability to accurately recall information decreases as the conversation becomes longer?
options: This is because the model automatically deletes old tokens after a certain period of time.
This is because all tokens look at each other, so the number of relationships increases as the square of the number of tokens, and attention is spread thinly.
This is because the moment the window limit is exceeded, the model suddenly stops working and ignores further input.
This is because it only appears on small models and disappears when you change to a larger model.
checks.explain: In Transformer, n tokens create n² relationships, so the longer the attention, the thinner the distribution. So context is a finite resource with diminishing marginal utility.

wrong.0: The model does not automatically delete tokens. Tokens entered as input are the subject of attention.
wrong.2: The drop appears as a gentle slope rather than a cliff.
wrong.3: The smoothness varies from model to model, but this property appears in all models.

checks.intro: Think about what causes foreground information to become blurred in long conversations. You will not be graded, so feel free to choose.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The reason is that when there are n tokens, there are n² relationships, which spreads attention thinly.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The cause is not deletion or interruption, but the structure of the distraction. Recall that as the number of tokens increases, the number of relationships increases squarely.

checks.q: Match the following terms and descriptions
right: A phenomenon in which the ability to accurately recall preceding information decreases as the number of tokens increases.
Cultivating the entire token set, including system instructions, tools, external data, and message records
A method of holding only identifiers such as file paths or links and loading them into a tool when needed.
Good at writing instructions, especially system prompts.
checks.explain: Prompt engineering is about refining instructions, and context engineering deals with all the tokens that go into a window. Context rot is a loss of precision in long contexts, and JIT context is one way to reduce this.
checks.intro: Match the four terms used in context management with explanations. It is not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Everything was connected correctly. The key is to distinguish between refining instructions and maintaining the entire window.
checks.incorrectFeedback: More than one pair was misaligned. Note the difference: prompt engineering refers to instructions, context engineering refers to all tokens entering a window, context rot refers to a phenomenon, and JIT refers to a response method.

checks.q: The research agent puts the text of all 50 search results into context, slowing down responses and obscuring the initial instructions. What is the most appropriate improvement?
options: Change to a model with a larger window so that all 50 items can fit.
Write more if-else rules into the system prompt so the model doesn't miss an instruction.
Leave only the title and link and open only what you need, leaving detailed navigation to the sub-agent.
As a result of already processing, the original text is left as is and only the order is moved back.
checks.explain: If low-relevant text is re-entered every turn, costs and delays increase, and context rot also worsens. JIT and subagent separation that only maintains identifiers reduce this.

wrong.0: Even if the window becomes larger, precision remains lower as the number of tokens increases, and costs and delays also increase.
wrong.1: Tangled rules are a structure that should be avoided and do not solve the problem of token waste.
wrong.3: The problem remains that the original text remains in the window and is re-entered every turn.

checks.intro: This is an example of 50 search results filling out the context. Pick which improvements address the root cause.
checks.correctFeedback: You chose well. By keeping only the identifier, recalling it when needed, and splitting navigation into subagents, we reduce the amount of tokens stacked up in the window.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Window size or adding rules will not solve the token stacking problem. Take a look at your view again based on the fact that if you keep the original text in the window it will be retyped every turn.

glossary.def: The range of tokens the model can process at one time. It's finite, and the longer it's not full, the more distracting it becomes.
It involves curating and maintaining a set of tokens at the point of inference, including system instructions, tools, external data, and message records.
This is a phenomenon in which the ability to accurately recall the information within the context decreases as the number of tokens in the context increases.
Rather than inserting data in advance, only the identifier is maintained, and when needed, it is loaded into the tool and placed in the context.
The structure is such that a sub-agent with a clean context takes charge of the search and returns only the summary to the main agent.
In long inputs, the model tends to utilize that information less accurately when the information it needs is in the middle rather than at the beginning or end. The degree varies from model to model.

misconceptions.myth: If the context window is large, you can put everything there.
misconceptions.fact: Even if the window is large, the precision remains gradually lower as the number of tokens increases. Triage is necessary because costs and delays also increase.

misconceptions.myth: Context engineering is like writing prompts well.
misconceptions.fact: The prompts are only part of the story. Context engineering covers the entire token, including tools, external data, and even message history.

misconceptions.myth: JIT context is always better than preload.
misconceptions.fact: Runtime searches are slower than precomputed searches. Therefore, hybrid methods where essential information is put in advance and the rest is found as a tool are common.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Context is a finite resource, and as tokens increase, marginal utility decreases.
The goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens that will produce the desired result.
The JIT context makes the window lightweight by leaving only the identifier and loading it when needed.
Subagent separation is a structure that isolates detailed navigation and returns only the summary.
